One beautiful Michigan summer, our families rented a cabin together near Traverse City. One day, we all made the trip to Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore.

I remember we had all made the long trek, including the famous steep climb down the dune, when someone realized something important had been left back in the car. I honestly can’t remember what the missing item was. What I do remember, clear as day, was Leroy and his selfless act. Without missing a beat, he volunteered to make the climb back up the dune, all the way to the car, and then back again to all of us. A journey that felt daunting enough to do once, he was happy to take on twice for the rest of us. That memory has always stuck with me and captures Leroy perfectly. Kind, always willing to go the extra mile for others (quite literally), and with enough stamina to make the rest of us question our life choices.

I also can’t leave out Leroy helping Molly and me produce our hit song, Swim, and even playing guitar on it. Not many adults are willing to spend that kind of quality time with kids, let alone help them bring their big creative ideas to life. At the time, it felt like the coolest thing ever… and honestly, it still does.

I’m so lucky to have Leroy Harvey in my life. Dear Leroy,
I have known you for a couple of decades. Although we have had very little direct communication over the years, the thought of you and the sight of you have made me smile consistently all these years.

The first time I noticed you was at the Fellowship when I happened to notice you and your young son, arms around one another, singing together from the hymnal. My thought was, “Who is that father? What a gift he is giving to his son by bringing him into this loving community and making music with him.”

After that, I always noticed you at the Fellowship and smiled at the sight of you.

Several years later, with little or no direct conversation, you blew my mind. Maybe you remember the event. I was working with the Michigan Department of Community Health on the “Walkable Communities” initiative. We had a representative of the CDC coming to see how Michigan was spending the grant money we’d been given by CDC, some of which had gone to the Allen Street Center. I drove him to a meeting you were having with all your sub grantees, at which you asked each person present to tell what their little bit of grant money. 

Maybe you remember what I told you about the CDC guy’s reaction to what he had heard from your grantees. He said, with a huge amount of enthusiasm, “Well, I am glad that my tax dollars are being used for these projects.“ I was glad that you had made us look good, but I was thrilled to see the creative used to which you had put the small amounts of money. They were all doing things that could really make a difference.

I’m not sure at what point I learned who your mother was. I could see where your concern for the environment came from. Knowing that she could sometimes be a bit challenging to be around, I was dazzled by your kindness and loving attitude toward her. I wasn’t present at the Fellowship when you gave a Mother’s Day tribute to her, but I heard about it. Wow.

The next time I noticed you was in the context of recycling. I’m not sure all the different roles you have played, but I felt my community was truly blessed by having you in a stewardship role for our environment. I’m sure none of those jobs paid a lot of money, I assumed that taking care of the environment was more of a vocation for you than a job.

The other context in which you made me smile was your musicianship. I saw you making music at the Fellowship and in a few other informal venues. Your choice of music and the sound you put out never failed to warm my heart and bring me joy.

I am sorry that my life path did not intersect more with yours. Truly, I have seen you as a Point of Light in the world. What you leave behind will not disappear when you are gone. 

With love,
Karen Petersmarck
